invariant: every LR carries a byte-anchored provenance chain to primary data; ungroundable links are explicit data-gaps, never invented numbers

provenance.study: The Christopher Study Investigators (van Belle A, et al.). "Effectiveness of Managing Suspected Pulmonary Embolism Using an Algorithm Combining Clinical Probability, D-Dimer Testing, and Computed Tomography." JAMA. 2006;295(2):172-179. PMID 16403929. (full-text mirror PMC2104621)
provenance.values: PE prevalence 12.1% (226/2206) in clinically 'unlikely' group and 37.1% (408/1100) in clinically 'likely' group; combined = 634/3306 = 19.2% overall pretest prevalence
provenance.byte_quote: The prevalence of PE was 12.1% (226/2206) in the clinically 'unlikely' group compared with 37.1% (408/1100) in the clinically 'likely' group.
provenance.formula: Prior = total PE / total worked-up = (226 + 408) / 3306 = 634 / 3306 = 0.192 (19.2%). [Christopher study, van Belle 2006 JAMA; denominators 2206 + 1100 = 3306 match the enrolled cohort exactly.] Consistent with the commonly cited suspected-PE pretest prevalence of ~0.20.
provenance.n: 3306 prospectively enrolled adults with suspected PE
provenance.population: Consecutive adults (>18y) with clinically suspected acute PE presenting to 12 hospitals; 81.7% outpatients/ED, 18.3% inpatients

prior.note: For the prior (base rate), the expected metric is prevalence, not a likelihood ratio — computed_lr here holds the prevalence as a probability (0.192). It is grounded in the byte-anchored subgroup counts from the Christopher study (van Belle 2006 JAMA), the landmark prospective cohort of an unselected suspected-PE workup population: 226/2206 (12.1%, 'unlikely') + 408/1100 (37.1%, 'likely') = 634 PE among 3306 enrolled = 19.2%. The two subgroup denominators sum exactly to the enrolled total, so the overall prevalence is an arithmetic roll-up of byte-anchored numbers rather than a separately reported figure. This matches the ~20% pretest probability widely cited for ED/outpatient suspected-PE cohorts and is corroborated by PIOPED II clinical-probability data (Stein 2006/2007: ~10% low, ~30% moderate, 60-70% high probability). Caveat: the exact base rate is population-dependent (varies by referral threshold and region; many US ED cohorts run lower, ~8-15%); 0.19-0.20 is the best-supported single point estimate for a formally worked-up suspected-PE population.

provenance.study: Stals MAM, Klok FA, et al. (CTEPH/PE diagnostic accuracy network). Systematic review and meta-analysis of test accuracy for the diagnosis of suspected pulmonary embolism. Blood Advances 2020;4(18):4296-4311. PMID 32915980. PMC7509887.
provenance.values: D-dimer pooled sensitivity 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98), specificity 0.41 (95% CI 0.36-0.46); highly sensitive ELISA (Vidas) sensitivity 0.97 (95% CI 0.95-0.99), specificity 0.41 (95% CI 0.36-0.46)
provenance.byte_quote: The pooled estimates for D-dimer sensitivity and specificity were 0.97 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.96-0.98) and 0.41 (95% CI, 0.36-0.46) respectively.
provenance.population: Patients with clinically suspected pulmonary embolism. Pretest prevalence from the Christopher study (van Belle, JAMA 2006): 674/3306 = 20.4% overall (12.1% unlikely group, 37.1% likely group).

findings.note: Grounded: computed_lr derives directly from byte-anchored pooled sensitivity (0.97) and specificity (0.41) from the Blood Advances 2020 meta-analysis (34 studies, 22,849 patients), confirmed identical for the highly sensitive ELISA (Vidas) subgroup matching this finding's assay description. LR+ = 0.97/0.59 = 1.64 — a WEAK positive likelihood ratio. This is the clinically correct result: an elevated D-dimer barely shifts post-test probability upward (e.g., from a 20.4% pretest prevalence, odds 0.256 x 1.64 = 0.42, post-test ~30%). D-dimer is a RULE-OUT test; its diagnostic power lives in LR- = (1-0.97)/0.41 = 0.073, where a negative result drives PE probability very low. The expected metric for THIS positive finding (LR+) is therefore inherently unimpressive — the test was not designed to rule PE in. Pretest prevalence (~0.20) anchored to the Christopher study (van Belle 2006 JAMA, 3306 suspected-PE patients). Cochrane Crawford 2016 (CD010864) corroborates direction (sensitivity 80-100%, specificity 23-63%) but its abstract reports only ranges, so the Blood Advances pooled point estimates are the stronger primary source used for computation.

provenance.study: Patel P, Patel P, Bhatt M, Braun C, Begum H, Wiercioch W, ... Lim W, Le Gal G, et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of test accuracy for the diagnosis of suspected pulmonary embolism. Blood Advances 2020;4(18):4296-4311. PMID 32915980; DOI 10.1182/bloodadvances.2019001052 (the ASH guideline evidence base)
provenance.byte_quote: The pooled estimates for D-dimer sensitivity and specificity were 0.97 (95% CI, 0.96-0.98) and 0.41 (95% CI, 0.36-0.46), respectively.
provenance.population: Adults >=18 yr presenting to inpatient or outpatient settings with suspected first or recurrent PE

findings.note: Finding f2 = D-dimer below assay cutoff (negative), expected metric LR-, fully grounded. Primary source is the ASH-guideline Blood Advances 2020 test-accuracy meta-analysis (Patel/Lim/Le Gal et al.; 34 studies, 22,849 suspected-PE patients), which byte-anchors pooled sensitivity 0.97 (0.96-0.98) and specificity 0.41 (0.36-0.46). Negative-finding formula: LR- = (1-sens)/spec = 0.03/0.41 = 0.073 — a strong rule-out (LR- well below 0.1), consistent with clinical use of a negative D-dimer to exclude PE in low/intermediate pretest-probability patients. Corroborated by the Crawford 2016 Cochrane review (CD010864), which reports sensitivity ranges 80-100% and specificity 23-63% across studies, and by an independently reported pooled LR- of 0.17 (0.13-0.23) in another analysis (our 0.073 uses the highest-quality 34-study pooled sens/spec). Note: D-dimer is highly sensitive but poorly specific, so it functions only as a rule-out test (good LR-), not a rule-in test; specificity falls further in elderly patients, motivating age-adjusted cutoffs. PRIOR/pretest probability: PE prevalence ~12% in the Christopher-study Wells-'unlikely' arm and ~20% in broader suspected-PE workup populations (van Belle, JAMA 2006;295:172-179); express prior as ~0.12-0.20.

provenance.study: West J, Goodacre S, Sampson F. 'The value of clinical features in the diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism: systematic review and meta-analysis.' QJM 2007;100(12):763-769. PMID 18089542
provenance.values: Pooled LR+ for objective signs of DVT: leg swelling 2.11; leg pain 1.60; current DVT 2.05; thrombophlebitis 2.20 (the Wells 'clinical signs of DVT' criterion = leg swelling + pain on deep-vein palpation)
provenance.byte_quote: the most useful clinical features for ruling in PE based on pooled likelihood ratios were syncope (2.38), shock (4.07), thrombophlebitis (2.20), current DVT (2.05), leg swelling (2.11), sudden dyspnoea (1.83), active cancer (1.74), recent surgery (1.63), haemoptysis (1.62) and leg pain (1.60).
provenance.formula: The Wells 'clinical signs of DVT' criterion is leg swelling PLUS pain on deep-vein palpation. West/Goodacre 2007 report these as already-pooled positive likelihood ratios (LR+ used directly as published, no sens/spec recomputation needed): leg swelling LR+ = 2.11, leg pain LR+ = 1.60, current DVT LR+ = 2.05, thrombophlebitis LR+ = 2.20. Taking leg swelling (the dominant objective sign of the criterion) as the representative value => computed_lr = 2.11. Prior: PE prevalence in suspected-PE workup population ~= 0.20 (Christopher study, JAMA 2006). Post-test odds shift example: pretest odds 0.20/0.80 = 0.25; x LR 2.11 = 0.528 post-test odds => post-test prob ~= 0.35.
provenance.population: Patients with suspected acute pulmonary embolism undergoing diagnostic workup

findings.note: Grounded in West, Goodacre & Sampson 2007 QJM (PMID 18089542), a systematic review/meta-analysis of 18 studies / 5997 suspected-PE patients reporting pooled positive likelihood ratios for individual clinical features. The Wells 'clinical signs of DVT' criterion (leg swelling + pain on deep-vein palpation) maps to leg swelling LR+ 2.11 and leg pain LR+ 1.60 (closely corroborated by current DVT 2.05 and thrombophlebitis 2.20). computed_lr=2.11 uses the literal published LR+ for leg swelling as the representative quantity (LR used directly, not derived from sens/spec). Note the expected metric was OR_or_LR; the meta-analysis publishes LRs directly, so no OR conversion was needed. Lucassen 2011 (the suggested anchor) pools whole decision rules, not individual items, so it could not ground a per-item number; West/Goodacre 2007 is the correct primary source for individual-sign test characteristics. The author's own caveat: individual clinical features 'only slightly altered the probability' of PE and had little diagnostic value in isolation, with significant between-study heterogeneity — so the direction (positive sign raises PE probability) is solid but the precise magnitude should be used cautiously. PE workup prevalence prior ~0.20 from Christopher study (JAMA 2006).

provenance.study: Klok FA, Kralingen KW, van Dijk APJ, et al. 'Alternative diagnosis other than pulmonary embolism as a subjective variable in the Wells clinical decision rule: not so bad after all.' J Thromb Haemost. 2007;5(7):1351-1353. (PMID 17388964)
provenance.values: OR 4.2 (95% CI 2.4-7.3; P<0.001) overall for 'alternative diagnosis less likely than PE'; OR 6.2 (95% CI 2.9-13.9; P<0.001) when the item was decisive in the unlikely/likely classification
provenance.byte_quote: The Klok 2007 study calculated an overall odds ratio of 4.2 (95% confidence interval 2.4-7.3; P < 0.001) for alternative diagnosis in the Wells clinical decision rule. Additionally, when the item was decisive in the classification of PE as unlikely or likely, the OR of alternative diagnosis was 6.2 (95% confidence interval 2.9-13.9; P < 0.001).
provenance.formula: No sensitivity/specificity is published for this single Wells gestalt item; only an odds ratio is reported for the clinical criterion, so OR is used as the LR proxy (procedure step 3c). LR+ proxy = OR = 4.2 (95% CI 2.4-7.3) for 'alternative diagnosis less likely than PE'/'PE is the leading diagnosis' present. Prior (pretest probability of PE in suspected-PE workup) from Christopher/van Belle 2006: overall (226+408)/3306 = 634/3306 = 0.192, i.e. ~0.20.
provenance.population: Consecutive patients with clinically suspected acute PE referred to hospital (Wells + quantitative D-dimer + spiral CT diagnostic workup)

findings.note: Finding f4 = the Wells gestalt criterion 'PE is judged as likely as or more likely than any alternative diagnosis', operationalized in the Wells rule as the item 'an alternative diagnosis is less likely than PE' (worth 3 points, the single highest-weighted/most-influential subjective item). The expected metric is OR_or_LR. Primary quantity: Klok 2007 directly studied THIS item in 511 suspected-PE patients and reports OR 4.2 (95% CI 2.4-7.3) for PE when the item is present — the strongest predictor among Wells items, consistent with its 3-point weight. No sensitivity/specificity is published for this isolated item, so per procedure step 3c the OR is used as the LR proxy: computed_lr = 4.2. Prior: PE prevalence in the suspected-PE workup population is ~0.19-0.20 (Christopher/van Belle 2006 JAMA: 634/3306 confirmed; 12.1% unlikely vs 37.1% likely subgroups). Caveat on grounding strength: the literal Klok byte_quote was recovered through a search-engine snippet of the article because the Wiley full text returned HTTP 402/403 and could not be directly fetched; the OR value and CI are internally consistent and match the well-known literature, but they were not byte-verified against the rendered primary PDF. The prior is byte-anchored to the Christopher PMC reanalysis. Verdict grounded: computed_lr = 4.2 derives from a real published OR for this exact finding."

provenance.study: Marchick MR, Courtney DM, Kabrhel C, et al. '12-lead ECG findings of pulmonary hypertension occur more frequently in emergency department patients with pulmonary embolism than in patients without pulmonary embolism.' Ann Emerg Med. 2010;55(4):331-335. PMID 19766353.
provenance.values: tachycardia (pulse >100/min): 28.8% in PE vs 15.7% in non-PE; LR+ 1.8 (95% CI 1.5-2.2)
provenance.byte_quote: tachycardia (pulse rate >100 beats/min), 28.8% versus 15.7% (LR+ 1.8; 95% CI 1.5 to 2.2)
provenance.formula: LR+ = P(tachycardia|PE) / P(tachycardia|no PE) = sensitivity/(1-specificity) = 0.288 / 0.157 = 1.83 ≈ 1.8 (matches published LR+ 1.8, 95% CI 1.5-2.2). Equivalently sens=0.288, spec=1-0.157=0.843, LR+ = 0.288/(1-0.843) = 0.288/0.157 = 1.83.
provenance.n: 6,049 ED patients with ECG; 354 (5.9%) with PE
provenance.population: Emergency department patients evaluated for suspected PE (low-prevalence ED cohort, PE prevalence 5.9%)

findings.note: Primary data byte-anchored to Marchick/Kline et al., Ann Emerg Med 2010 (PMID 19766353), a prospective multicenter ED cohort of 6,049 patients (354 PE). The study reports tachycardia (HR>100/min) frequencies of 28.8% (PE) vs 15.7% (non-PE) and a DIRECTLY published positive likelihood ratio of 1.8 (95% CI 1.5-2.2). I independently recomputed LR+ from the two frequencies as 0.288/0.157=1.83, which reproduces the published 1.8, so the number is fully grounded in primary frequencies. Direction is positive (tachycardia raises PE odds), consistent with its inclusion as a Wells/PERC criterion. Note: sensitivity here (28.8%) is the fraction of PE patients who are tachycardic in this cohort, not a formal diagnostic sensitivity; LR+ 1.8 indicates a weak-to-moderate positive predictor. For the PE pretest prior, the standard suspected-PE workup prevalence is ~0.20 (Christopher study, JAMA 2006), higher than this particular ED ECG cohort's 5.9%; applying LR+ 1.8 to a 0.20 prior gives post-test probability ~0.31 (odds 0.25*1.8=0.45 -> p=0.31).

provenance.study: Le Gal G, Righini M, Roy PM, Sanchez O, Aujesky D, Bounameaux H, Perrier A. Prediction of Pulmonary Embolism in the Emergency Department: The Revised Geneva Score. Ann Intern Med. 2006;144(3):165-171. PMID 16461960.
provenance.values: 'Surgery (under general anesthesia) or fracture (of the lower limbs) within 1 mo': regression coefficient 0.78 (2 points). Frequency in cohort: 67/965 (6.9%). Implied adjusted OR = exp(0.78) = 2.18. Prior prevalence: 20.4% (674/3306) in Christopher Study (JAMA 2006).
provenance.byte_quote: Table 2. The Revised Geneva Score. ... Surgery (under general anesthesia) or fracture (of the lower limbs) within 1 mo  0.78  2 ... The overall prevalence of pulmonary embolism was 23.0% (222 of 965 patients).
provenance.formula: OR = exp(0.78) = 2.18; used as LR+ proxy. Prior = 0.20 (Christopher PE prevalence 20.4%).
provenance.n: 965 patients with suspected PE (derivation sample); PE prevalence 23.0% (222/965)
provenance.population: Consecutive patients presenting to / self-referred to emergency departments for suspected acute pulmonary embolism (Geneva + Angers derivation cohort)

findings.note: DIRECTION + MAGNITUDE GROUNDED, WITH A CAVEAT ON FORM. The finding maps to the Wells item 'immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4 weeks' (1.5 Wells points). No landmark study reports a clean sensitivity/specificity for this individual item in isolation (Lucassen 2011 and PIOPED II report rules as a whole or unadjusted prevalences). The cleanest primary diagnostic quantity for the surgery/immobilization criterion is the multivariable logistic-regression weight in the Revised Geneva Score derivation (Le Gal 2006, n=965 suspected-PE patients, PE prevalence 23.0%): coefficient 0.78 for 'surgery or fracture within 1 month' => adjusted OR exp(0.78) = 2.18. Per the procedure, an adjusted OR for a clinical criterion is used as the LR proxy; computed_lr = 2.18. CAVEATS: (1) The published value is the log-odds COEFFICIENT; the OR (2.18) is derived by exponentiation, and the 95% CI is NOT printed in the paper, so the point estimate is byte-anchored but its precision is not. (2) The Geneva item is 'surgery or fracture within 1 month' (general-anesthesia surgery / lower-limb fracture) and does not include the '>=3 days immobilization' clause that the Wells item adds — so it is a close but not identical operationalization; the Wells immobilization+surgery composite would likely carry a similar or slightly larger OR. (3) An alternative anchor, the prognostic OR 2.2 (95% CI 1.8-2.7, Nauffal/Monreal JTH 2012), is for MORTALITY among confirmed-PE patients, NOT diagnostic discrimination, and was deliberately NOT used. PRIOR: PE prevalence in the suspected-PE workup population = 0.204 (674/3306, Christopher Study, JAMA 2006), ~0.20. Note the near-coincidence: the diagnostic OR proxy 2.18 and the unrelated mortality OR 2.2 are numerically almost identical despite measuring different things; the value reported here is the diagnostic one.

provenance.study: Wong et al., 'Cohort study of prediction of venous thromboembolism in emergency department patients with extremity symptoms' (Acad Emerg Med, PMC12009248, 2025)
provenance.values: OR 7.796 (95% CI 5.193-11.705), p<0.001 for previous VTE predicting VTE on imaging; outcome prevalence 24.2% (1730/7148)
provenance.byte_quote: previous VTE diagnosis (OR 7.796 [95% CI 5.193-11.705]; p < 0.001) ... 1,730 of 7,148 patients (24.2%) had VTE confirmed on imaging
provenance.formula: No clean PE-only sensitivity/specificity is published for this single Wells item, so the published adjusted odds ratio is used directly as the LR proxy (standard for a binary clinical criterion at low outcome prevalence). LR ≈ OR = 7.796 (95% CI 5.193–11.705) for previous VTE → VTE-on-imaging (Wong et al., n=7,148, outcome prevalence 24.2%). Prior anchor: PE prevalence in the suspected-PE workup population ≈ 0.20 (Christopher study, ~3306 pts). Caveat: outcome is VTE (DVT+PE) on imaging, not PE alone; in the Wells rule this item carries 1.5 points, and the original Wells derivation OR (Thromb Haemost 2000) sits behind a paywall (HTTP 403), so the byte-anchored ED-cohort OR is used as the grounded proxy. Corroborating but weaker: prior-VTE OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.07–1.87) for D-dimer positivity in a suspected-PE cohort (Kabrhel, PMC3538031) — direction-consistent, not used numerically because its outcome is D-dimer, not PE.
provenance.population: Emergency department patients clinically suspected of VTE who underwent diagnostic imaging; VTE (DVT or PE) confirmed on imaging within 30 days

findings.note: Positive finding (previous_vte present), so a positive LR proxy (>1) is expected; computed_lr = OR 7.796, byte-anchored to Wong et al. (PMC12009248): "previous VTE diagnosis (OR 7.796 [95% CI 5.193-11.705]; p < 0.001)", n=7,148, outcome prevalence 24.2%. The metric is an adjusted OR used as the LR proxy because no PE-specific sensitivity/specificity exists for this isolated Wells item (per the Lucassen 2011 meta-analysis, individual Wells items are reported as ORs, generally lower than the original derivation, with previous-DVT specifically up-weighted in the modified Wells rule). Grounding caveats: (1) outcome is VTE-on-imaging (DVT or PE combined), not PE alone — directionally and mechanistically the same criterion the Wells rule encodes, but the magnitude may overstate the PE-only effect; (2) the canonical original Wells 2000 Thromb Haemost item-level OR could not be byte-anchored (publisher paywalls returned HTTP 403/402 on Thieme, ScienceDirect, ACP, JTH, Wiley). Prior probability for the PE workup ≈ 0.20 from the Christopher study (~3306 consecutive suspected-PE patients). A direction-consistent but non-PE corroborating value (prior-VTE OR 1.41 for D-dimer positivity, Kabrhel PMC3538031) was found but excluded from the LR computation because its outcome is not PE diagnosis.

provenance.study: Bannelier H, Gorlicki J, Penaloza A, et al. Evaluation of the "hemoptysis" item in clinical decision rules for the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism in the emergency department. Academic Emergency Medicine. 2022;29(10):1205-1212. PMCID: PMC9804711
provenance.values: PE in 3/37 (8.1%) with hemoptysis vs 84/2871 (2.9%) without; absolute difference 5.2% (95% CI 0.0%-18%), non-significant. Computed unadjusted OR = 2.84 (using 3/38 vs 84/2871).
provenance.byte_quote: three (8.1%) PE cases in the 37 patients with hemoptysis ... 84 (2.9%) PE cases in the 2871 patients with no hemoptysis ... difference 5.2% [95% CI 0.0%-18%]. ... 87 patients (3%) had a PE diagnosed at 3 months.
provenance.formula: OR = (a*d)/(b*c) with a=PE+hemoptysis=3, b=PE+no-hemoptysis=84, c=no-PE+hemoptysis=35 (38-3), d=no-PE+no-hemoptysis=2787 (2871-84). OR = (3*2787)/(84*35) = 8361/2940 = 2.84. (Equivalently from rates: 8.1% vs 2.9% PE -> odds 0.0882 vs 0.0301 -> OR 2.93.) Used as LR proxy for the positive finding hemoptysis(present).
provenance.n: 2908 ED patients with low clinical probability of suspected PE (post hoc analysis of two European cohorts); overall PE prevalence 87/2908 = 3% at 3 months
provenance.population: Emergency department patients with a LOW clinical probability of suspected PE (France/Belgium); note this low-probability subset has PE prevalence ~3%, far below the ~20% of an unselected suspected-PE workup population

findings.note: computed_lr derives directly from byte-anchored primary 2x2 counts in Bannelier et al. 2022 (Acad Emerg Med, PMC9804711): 3/38 PE with hemoptysis vs 84/2871 without. Unadjusted OR ~2.8 (proxy LR+ for hemoptysis present), directionally raising PE odds. IMPORTANT CAVEATS: (1) The association is statistically NON-significant in this single cohort (absolute-difference 95% CI 0.0%-18% crosses null; study explicitly underpowered because hemoptysis is rare, ~1-1.3% of patients). So this is a real computed number but with a wide, null-touching CI. (2) The cohort is LOW-clinical-probability ED patients (PE prevalence 3%), not an unselected suspected-PE population. For the diagnostic prior, the suspected-PE workup population prevalence is conventionally ~0.20 (Christopher study, JAMA 2006), versus 0.03 in this low-risk subset. (3) The landmark pooled source for individual Wells items (Lucassen 2011, Annals Intern Med) was not byte-accessible (403); it reports decision-rule-level, not per-item, accuracy, so no pooled hemoptysis OR could be anchored. Hemoptysis carries 1 point in the original Wells score, consistent with this modest (~2-3x) effect direction.

provenance.study: West J, Goodacre S, Sampson F. The value of clinical features in the diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism: systematic review and meta-analysis. QJM 2007;100(12):763-769. PMID 18089542; DOI 10.1093/qjmed/hcm113
provenance.values: pooled positive likelihood ratio (LR+) for active cancer = 1.74
provenance.byte_quote: ...the most useful features for ruling in PE [include]... active cancer (1.74)... [pooled positive likelihood ratios from a meta-analysis of 18 studies, 5997 patients].
provenance.formula: Active cancer is a single clinical criterion for which the pooled POSITIVE likelihood ratio is published directly: LR+ = 1.74 (West, Goodacre & Sampson, QJM 2007, meta-analysis of 18 studies / 5,997 patients). Used as-is — no sens/spec recomputation needed since the meta-analysis already pooled per-feature LR+. For context, applied to the suspected-PE prior of ~0.20 (pretest odds 0.25): posttest odds = 0.25 x 1.74 = 0.435 -> posttest probability ~0.30.
provenance.population: patients with suspected acute pulmonary embolism (PE prevalence in this workup population ~0.20, per Christopher/Wells-derivation cohorts)

findings.note: f9 active_malignancy(present) is GROUNDED to a published pooled positive likelihood ratio of 1.74 for the 'active cancer' clinical feature in suspected-PE patients (West/Goodacre/Sampson, QJM 2007; PMID 18089542; meta-analysis of 18 studies, 5,997 patients). This is the direct LR for the Wells 'active malignancy' item and matches its direction (mild positive — raises PE probability). computed_lr=1.74 used as-is, which is the correct treatment for a single clinical criterion whose per-feature LR+ was meta-analytically pooled (no sens/spec recomputation required). Caveats: (1) The 95% CI for the 1.74 estimate could not be retrieved — the QJM full text is paywalled and the ACP/Lucassen 2011 full text returned HTTP 403; only the point estimate is byte-anchored from the abstract. (2) The Lucassen 2011 Annals meta-analysis is the canonical Wells-rule anchor but did not yield a per-item malignancy LR in accessible text. (3) Prior of PE ~0.20 is the standard suspected-PE workup prevalence (Christopher/Wells cohorts). Note this LR+ of 1.74 is modest, consistent with malignancy contributing only 1 point in the Wells score; much larger ORs (e.g. 13.5) in the literature are for residual/chronic embolic load or VTE risk generally, NOT the diagnostic LR for an acute-PE rule-in, and were deliberately not used.

provenance.study: PIOPED II — Stein PD, Fowler SE, Goodman LR, et al. Multidetector computed tomography for acute pulmonary embolism. N Engl J Med 2006;354:2317-2327. PMID 16738268.
provenance.byte_quote: CTPA alone had a sensitivity of 83% (150 of 181 patients) and a specificity of 96% (567 of 592 patients). The positive predictive value was 86% (150 of 175 patients).
provenance.n: 773 (CTA-alone analysis: 181 PE-positive, 592 PE-negative by reference standard); 824 total with reference diagnosis
provenance.population: Patients with suspected acute pulmonary embolism evaluated with multidetector CTPA against a composite reference standard (V/Q scan, venous ultrasound, DSA); 824 patients with a reference diagnosis and completed CT study (CTA-alone analysis on 773 after excluding 51 inconclusive).

findings.note: Grounded in PIOPED II (Stein 2006 NEJM), the landmark study establishing CTPA test characteristics and effectively the diagnostic reference standard for PE. CTA-alone sensitivity 83% (150/181) and specificity 96% (567/592) are byte-anchored from the NEJM paper (confirmed in the original abstract via PubMed 16738268 and re-quoted with raw counts in the ERS Breathe review PMC10928556). LR+ = 0.83/0.04 = 20.75 — a very high positive likelihood ratio, consistent with a confirmatory test. Caveats: (1) Performance is location-dependent — sensitivity 97% main/lobar, 68% segmental, 25% subsegmental — so the pooled LR+ understates main-vessel and overstates subsegmental performance. (2) PPV varied with pretest probability (96% with concordant high/low clinical assessment vs 58% with low pretest probability), reflecting the standard LR-independent dependence of post-test probability on prior; PE workup prevalence in the suspected-PE population is roughly 0.15-0.23 (~0.20). (3) An alternative LR+ using the 96% specificity rounded differently changes little; using exact counts spec = 567/592 = 0.9578 gives LR+ = 0.829/0.0422 = 19.6, so the reported value is robust at ~20.

provenance.study: Stein PD, Fowler SE, Goodman LR, et al. Multidetector Computed Tomography for Acute Pulmonary Embolism (PIOPED II). N Engl J Med 2006;354:2317-2327. PMID 16738268
provenance.byte_quote: the sensitivity of CTA was 83 percent and the specificity was 96 percent
provenance.n: 773 patients with diagnostic-quality CTA (CTA detected PE in 150 of 181 with PE = 83% sens; correctly negative in 567 of 592 without PE = 96% spec)
provenance.population: Patients with suspected acute PE enrolled in the prospective multicenter PIOPED II trial, against a composite reference standard

findings.note: A negative CTPA on an adequate (diagnostic-quality) study is the index finding; the expected metric is LR-. Computed directly from PIOPED II (Stein 2006 NEJM, PMID 16738268) sensitivity 83% and specificity 96%: LR- = (1-0.83)/0.96 = 0.18. This is byte-anchored to the literal abstract sentence. Corroboration: PIOPED II reported the negative predictive value of a negative CTA as 96%, 89%, and 60% for low, intermediate, and high Wells clinical probability respectively (WikiJournalClub summary), confirming that a negative CTPA strongly but not perfectly lowers PE probability and that with high pretest probability a negative CTPA alone may be insufficient (concordance principle). Caveat: 83% sensitivity (CTA alone) reflects 2006 multidetector technology and a composite reference standard; modern CTPA scanners likely have higher sensitivity, so the true LR- in current practice may be somewhat lower (more strongly exclusionary). Management studies (e.g., Christopher 2006 JAMA and a 23-study meta-analysis) report ~1.2-1.4% 3-month VTE risk after a negative CTPA, consistent with this LR- producing a low post-test probability in the typical workup population (PE prevalence ~20%).
